title: Indian-American Congressman Calls Livestreamed Execution 'Blatantly Un-American'
excerpt: Rep. Suhas Subramanyam condemned the Pentagon's plan to broadcast Nidal Hasan's firing-squad execution and demanded Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's removal.
body:
• Indian-American Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-Virginia) on Friday condemned the Pentagon's announced plan to livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan, calling it “blatantly un-American” and demanding the removal of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
  • “Regimes in Iran, North Korea, and ISIS carry out public executions, not America,” Subramanyam said in a statement, arguing the broadcast would damage America's moral standing and set a dangerous precedent.
  • The backlash is now bipartisan: Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on whether the livestream would happen and said he would not watch it, while President Trump said the administration was “making a determination” on the broadcast.
  • Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 at Fort Hood, Texas, in November 2009, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3 at 1 pm local time — the first public execution in the US since 1936.

Indian-American Congressman Suhas Subramanyam has condemned the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of the Fort Hood mass shooter, calling the proposed broadcast “blatantly un-American” and demanding that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth be removed.

Subramanyam, a Democrat representing Virginia's 10th Congressional District and the ranking member of the House Oversight Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs, issued the statement on Friday after the Pentagon announced that Nidal Malik Hasan's execution by firing squad would be shown to the public.

“Regimes in Iran, North Korea, and ISIS carry out public executions, not America. Nidal Malik Hasan should face consequences, but livestreaming his execution is blatantly un-American.”

— Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.)

“When we do this, we lose our moral standing on the global stage and set a horrible precedent,” Subramanyam added. “The Administration must stop this, and Secretary Hegseth needs to be removed. History will not judge this action kindly.” His criticism focused on the proposed public broadcast rather than on opposing punishment for Hasan's crimes.

How the plan emerged

Hegseth confirmed the livestream plan on Thursday during an interview with podcaster Jack Posobiec aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln. “We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth said, according to CNN.

The announcement was swiftly met with bipartisan outrage. Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday over whether the execution would actually be livestreamed — “I don't know that that's actually going to happen” — and said he would not watch it. Speaking to reporters Friday evening, President Donald Trump said the administration would make a determination about the livestream. FCC chair Brendan Carr said it was his understanding the execution would not be shown on broadcast television, but deferred to Hegseth.

Army regulations limit who may witness executions — barring anyone under 18 — and there is no formal provision for livestreaming the punishment. The US Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the plan as “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death.” The last public execution in America is considered to be the 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky — nearly 90 years ago.

The case behind the controversy

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Fort Hood Soldier Readiness Center in Killeen, Texas, on November 5, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 before he was subdued. A military court sentenced him to death, and he is set to be executed by firing squad on December 3 at Fort Hood — now known as Fort Cavazos — at 1 pm local time. Firing squads are rare in the US, used sparingly as an alternative to lethal injection.

Diaspora angle

Subramanyam's statement puts an Indian-American congressional voice at the centre of one of the week's most charged American debates — and it matters for diaspora families who track how capital punishment, military justice and media spectacle intersect in their adopted country. His framing — that public executions are what authoritarian regimes do, not democracies — is likely to resonate well beyond the Indian-American community.

What's next

With the White House still “making a determination” and the December 3 date approaching, the question is whether the Pentagon formalises the livestream plan or quietly retreats under bipartisan and now congressional pressure. Democrats have already renewed calls for Hegseth's removal and floated impeachment if they retake the House in November — making the execution broadcast a live political fight, not just a military procedure.
